citation: Success for All®. (2017). WWC Intervention Report: Beginning Reading. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.successforall.org/
title: SFA® ability-grouped 90-minute daily reading block with sequenced phonics-to-comprehension instruction
description: SFA® elementary reading programs "combine cooperative-learning strategies with detailed lessons, which incorporate multimedia, puppet skits, and videos to support students' engagement and classroom instruction." Students in prekindergarten through first grade participate in Reading Roots, and students in second grade and above participate in Reading Wings. Students are grouped into reading classes of 15–20 students with others of similar reading ability, regardless of age or grade level, during a daily 90-minute reading period; regrouping by demonstrated improvement lets teachers teach the whole class without smaller within-class groups. Instruction is sequenced across several years, emphasizing phonemic awareness initially and broader reading skills later, with daily tutoring for struggling readers.
requirements: Certified teachers or paraprofessionals to provide daily tutoring to students who have difficulty reading at the same level as their classmates
Regrouping structures that allow reading classes of 15–20 students of similar ability across age or grade levels
constraints: The review focuses on the literacy component implemented within the whole-school reform program, so most students also received other program components
target_learning_goals: phonemic awareness, phonics, listening and speaking vocabulary, reading comprehension, and composition writing
examples: Teachers begin the period by reading children's storybooks aloud and discussing them; in grades 2–5 teachers use structured interactive activities built around partner reading and cooperative learning
key_sources: Success for All®. (2017). WWC Intervention Report: Beginning Reading. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/672

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Success for All
citation: Success for All program evidence summary. (2015). https://www.successforall.org
title: Regroup students across grade lines by current reading level using frequent curriculum-based assessment
description: Within Success for All, "children are frequently assessed on curriculum-based measures, and these are used to regroup children into reading groups according to current reading level, across grade lines." This keeps reading instruction matched to each child's current level rather than to grade placement, and pairs with one-to-one or small-group tutoring for struggling students, especially first graders.
requirements: Frequent curriculum-based assessment of reading level
Flexibility to form reading groups across grade lines
target_learners: K-5 students in high-poverty elementary schools, especially struggling early readers
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading skills matched to current reading level
examples: Beginning with phonetically-controlled mini-books in grades K-1, with cooperative learning used extensively at all grade levels
key_sources: Success for All program evidence summary. (2015). https://www.successforall.org

article_title: Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice
citation: Haiwen Chu, Monique Evans. (2025). Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice. National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Systemic functional linguistics genre continua (mode, tenor, field) as an account of long-term language development
description: The brief draws on systemic functional linguistics, whose "fundamental premise" is considering "how language use is embedded in social purposes." Genres serve particular purposes and include continua of mode (dialogic-to-monologic organization), tenor (peer-to-authoritative relations), and field (everyday-to-technical topics). The authors use these continua to characterize how learners over time become more monologic, authoritative, and technical, and to interpret RAMPUP student language samples.
requirements: Language growth requires meaningful opportunities over sustained periods of time, per the brief
constraints: The brief applies the continua to secondary mathematics contexts with English Learners
target_learning_goals: academic language development alongside mathematical concepts
key_sources: Haiwen Chu, Monique Evans. (2025). Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice. National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED674747

article_title: Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity through the Every Student Succeeds Act
citation: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa
title: San Francisco International High School as a case of the four pillars serving new immigrant English learners
description: San Francisco International High School (SFIHS), part of the Internationals Network for Public Schools, serves new immigrant English learners; in 2015, "82% of students were classified as newcomers, and 35% were classified as non-readers in their native languages." The school requires an "activity-based curriculum" with projects, internships, and college-preparatory coursework for all students from day one, and evaluates students through portfolios showcased and defended twice per year. The report presents it as the four pillars operating at school, district, and state levels.
requirements: Portfolio assessment requiring students to write about, revise, and present their learning before teachers, staff, peers, and community members
constraints: The report presents this as a single school case rather than an experimental evaluation
examples: More than three-quarters of students in each of the school's first two graduating classes met the rigorous requirements for admissions to California's state university system, and 83% of 2013-14 graduates were enrolled in college in fall 2014
key_sources: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa

article_title: Universal Preschool in California: Promising Practices for Mixed Delivery Systems
citation: Melnick, H., Wechsler, M. E., Wang, V., & Plasencia, S. (2026). Universal preschool in California: Promising practices for mixed delivery systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/724.211
title: San Francisco Department of Early Childhood and Early Learning for All network
description: The San Francisco Department of Early Childhood (DEC) is a dedicated local governing agency for early childhood, reporting to the mayor, formed in 2013 and renamed in 2022 when it merged with First 5 San Francisco. It uses city funds, including Proposition C commercial rent tax revenue generating $180 million to $220 million annually with 85% dedicated to ECE, to incentivize providers to join its Early Learning for All network. In 2025 the network included 174 centers and 363 family child care providers; members must meet DEC's quality standards, accept subsidy children, and provide data, and in return receive supplemental funding, wage supplements, professional development and coaching, and family referrals.
requirements: Providers must meet DEC's quality standards, which are higher than most federal and state requirements
Providers must agree to accept children receiving child care subsidies and provide data regularly to DEC
constraints: San Francisco is the only case study site able to raise teacher qualifications and compensation at scale, due to its local commercial tax
target_learners: Children birth to age 5 in San Francisco
Families with low and moderate incomes
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to high-quality preschool and child care
examples: In 2022-23, the city funded 7,308 preschool and child care slots, of which 57% were for preschool-age children, 19% for toddlers, and 23% for infants.
key_sources: Melnick, H., Wechsler, M. E., Wang, V., & Plasencia, S. (2026). Universal preschool in California: Promising practices for mixed delivery systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/724.211

article_title: The Six-Facet Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire (SFAILQ): Assessing AI Literacy in Adolescents, Young Adults, and Midlife Adults
citation: Liu Qingqi, Miao Wenjiao, Li Jingjing, Lei Yuju. (2026). The Six-Facet Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire (SFAILQ): Assessing AI Literacy in Adolescents, Young Adults, and Midlife Adults. Behavioral Sciences, 16(7), 1110. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071110
title: SFAILQ: 32-item Six-Facet Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire
description: The SFAILQ is a 32-item self-report questionnaire assessing six AI literacy dimensions: affective experiences (5 items), usage skills (5 items), cognitive evaluation (6 items), ethical norms (6 items), responsible use (4 items), and self-development (6 items). It was developed with 2443 Chinese participants aged 12 to 60 using a random split-half design: item reduction on Sample 1 (N = 1217) and reliability/validity testing on Sample 2 (N = 1226). The article reports it "demonstrated high internal consistency, construct validity, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and criterion-related validity."
requirements: Administration with participants aged 12–60; items worded to suit both adolescents and adults (e.g., "in study or work" rather than workplace-only phrasing)
constraints: Scalar invariance ΔCFI approached the 0.01 threshold, so the authors advise cautious interpretation of mean comparisons across age groups
target_learning_goals: measuring AI literacy across six dimensions
examples: Validated against academic self-efficacy (ASES-C) and academic engagement (Utrecht Work Engagement Scale–Student–9) as criterion variables
key_sources: Liu Qingqi, Miao Wenjiao, Li Jingjing, Lei Yuju. (2026). The Six-Facet Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire (SFAILQ): Assessing AI Literacy in Adolescents, Young Adults, and Midlife Adults. Behavioral Sciences, 16(7), 1110. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071110

article_title: The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students
citation: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1
title: Consider sound field amplification important support in classrooms that do not meet recommended acoustic standards
description: The authors conclude that, although SFA did not produce measurable reading fluency gains for the general student body in this study, "SFA should be considered important support in classrooms that do not meet recommended acoustic standards". Amplification advanced fluency development for students with lower intellectual abilities while having no negative consequences for other students, and it improves access to the teacher's voice and reduces teacher voice strain.
requirements: Classrooms whose occupied noise levels and SNRs fall below recommended acoustic standards, such as the +15 dB minimum the article cites.
constraints: Reading fluency benefits were not demonstrated for the general 8–10-year-old student population in this study; translational academic impact is suggested to apply particularly to younger year levels.
target_learners: mainstream primary school students, particularly those with lower cognitive abilities or listening difficulties
target_learning_goals: protecting reading fluency development and access to spoken instruction in noisy classrooms
examples: In this study, 23 Victorian classrooms with occupied noise levels around 65 dBA used Front Row Juno systems, alternating between SFA-On and SFA-Off terms.
key_sources: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1

article_title: The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance
citation: Mandana Eftekhar Paziraie. (2013). The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance. English Language Teaching; Vol. 6, No. 2; 2013. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p71
title: Halliday's Systemic Functional Grammar and the textual metafunction as the resource creating coherence and cohesion in texts
description: The article presents Systemic Functional Grammar, in which Halliday (1970, 1985) introduces three metafunctions of language: ideational, interpersonal, and textual. Within this framework, the textual metafunction is "the one in which language as a discourse is organized to function as a complete message", with Theme as the departure point of the message and Rheme as the part where the Theme is developed. The article states that coherence and cohesion are created in a discourse through the textual metafunction, and uses this framework as the basis for its instructional treatment. Eggins is cited as holding that without the textual metafunction, experiential and interpersonal meanings cannot be expressed coherently.
requirements: The framework presupposes Halliday's tristratal construct of semantics, lexicogrammar, and phonology, organized by the paradigmatic notion of choice
constraints: The article notes viewpoints on coherence and cohesion differ among scholars, with common themes but disagreement on what the two elements are and how they connect
target_learning_goals: writing coherence and cohesion in English essays
examples: The training pamphlet's textual metafunction section taught Theme and Rheme, with exercises asking participants to underline the Theme and Rheme in sentences
key_sources: Mandana Eftekhar Paziraie. (2013). The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance. English Language Teaching; Vol. 6, No. 2; 2013. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p71

article_title: Success for All: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Sarah Miller, Andy Biggart, Seaneen Sloan, Liam O'Hare. (2017). Success for All: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Success for All (SfA) whole-school literacy programme
description: Success for All is a multi-component, whole-school literacy programme for primary schools underpinned by cooperative learning pedagogy, developed in the US and introduced to the UK in 1997. As the report describes it, "Success for All (SfA) is a whole-school approach to improving literacy in primary schools", with teacher training in group learning strategies, phonics and assessment, structured daily lesson plans, ongoing assessment, ability grouping, parental engagement, and leadership support. Delivery involves 16 days of training and support over two years, with stages comprising Kinder Corner (Reception), Roots and Wings (Years 1–6, 90-minute daily literacy sessions).
requirements: Whole-school delivery including all teachers and teaching assistants, with 2 days of initial whole-school training and 14 days of ongoing in-school support
A member of experienced teaching staff acting as the school's SfA coordinator to work with all staff to help ensure optimal implementation
constraints: Some schools found the programme prescriptive and adapted its content and delivery; of 27 intervention schools, 7 dropped out completely and 5 did not implement to the minimum expected level
Costs approximately £46,500 per school in the first year and £61.90 per pupil per year averaged over three years for a 275-pupil school
target_learners: Primary school pupils, particularly those in schools with high levels of deprivation
target_learning_goals: Early literacy: vocabulary, phonemic awareness, word identification, word attack, passage comprehension and phonics skills
examples: In the trial, the programme was delivered over two academic years on a whole-school basis by teachers and classroom assistants trained and supported by the Success for All Foundation, with schools receiving 16 days of training and support
key_sources: Sarah Miller, Andy Biggart, Seaneen Sloan, Liam O'Hare. (2017). Success for All: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581417

article_title: Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students' Thematic Choice in Academic Writing
citation: Wei, J. (2016). Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students’ Thematic Choice in Academic Writing. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(14). http://www.iiste.org
title: Systemic Functional Linguistic Theme typology: topical, textual and interpersonal Themes, with topical Themes divided into marked and unmarked
description: The article adopts Halliday's Systemic Functional Grammar definition of Theme as "point of departure of the message", recognized because it "is put in the first position", followed by the Rheme. Following SFG it distinguishes three Theme types in terms of textual metafunction — topical, textual (continuatives, conjunctions, conjunctive adjuncts), and interpersonal (vocatives, modal adjuncts, mood-markings) — and two topical types in terms of thematic markedness: unmarked (Theme mapped onto subject in declaratives) and marked Themes, further analyzed as spatial, temporal, manner, cause and contingency subtypes. The study uses this typology as its analytical framework for coding 120 essays at T-unit level.
requirements: Theme/Rheme division drawn after the first experiential constituent (the topical Theme), following Halliday (2014, p. 91)
T-unit used as the basic unit of analysis
constraints: The article notes alternative definitions of Theme exist (Berry, 1995; Forey, 2002; North, 2005) but adopts Halliday's
Opinion clauses such as I think are categorized as interpersonal Themes via grammatical metaphor, the metaphorical interpretation being adopted
target_learners: Chinese college English majors writing academic English
target_learning_goals: Organizing information and shaping texts through thematic choice in academic English writing
examples: Essays were coded by locating and numbering each T-unit, marking Theme/Rheme division with a slash, identifying Theme types, and counting raw numbers and proportions of TP patterns
key_sources: Wei, J. (2016). Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students’ Thematic Choice in Academic Writing. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(14). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102949

article_title: Effect of mental imagery using cognitive aids on the performance of novice anesthesiology residents during a simulated cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
citation: Levy Manon, Dopff Cécile, Audibert Gerard, Bouquet Antoine, Gurda Thomas, Sy Mohammed, Bleuze Pauline, Michelet Daphné. (2025). Effect of mental imagery using cognitive aids on the performance of novice anesthesiology residents during a simulated cardiopulmonary resuscitation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07782-8
title: SFAR cognitive aids for cardiopulmonary arrest
description: The SFAR (French Society of Anesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine) cognitive aids for cardiopulmonary arrest are expert-validated, step-by-step decision supports used as the content of the mental imagery intervention. The article states that "Cognitive aids provide valuable support in critical situations in anesthesia and intensive care, offering easy-to-use, step-by-step, real-time solutions", and that their progressive structure and ease of use make them particularly suitable for mental imagery. They were introduced during debriefing of the initial simulation training day and animated in a PowerPoint for the guided imagery session.
requirements: Introduced during debriefing after asystole and ventricular fibrillation scenarios so residents associate the aid with the resuscitation steps.
constraints: The aids are specific to cardiopulmonary arrest situations in anesthesia and intensive care as described in the article.
target_learning_goals: management of cardiopulmonary resuscitation, including non-technical skills in critical events
key_sources: Levy Manon, Dopff Cécile, Audibert Gerard, Bouquet Antoine, Gurda Thomas, Sy Mohammed, Bleuze Pauline, Michelet Daphné. (2025). Effect of mental imagery using cognitive aids on the performance of novice anesthesiology residents during a simulated cardiopulmonary resuscitation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07782-8
